8/S0/F0.text: The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

8/S0/F1.text: There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

8/S0/F2.text: The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.

8/S1/F0.text: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

8/S1/F1.text: Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.

8/S1/F2.text: Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement.

8/S1/F3.text: Surrounding, as a quality of immersion, is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or the extent of auditory source perception, and a wide field of view produces a more surrounding experience than a narrow field of view.

8/S1/F4.text: Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

8/S1/F5.text: Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

8/S1/F6.text: Plot-informing, as a quality of immersion, means the experience is a scripted story, and the more the user can understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and the overall story, including its consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities, the more plot-informing the experience is.

8/S1/F7.text: In virtual reality (VR), immersion is the technological issue and presence is the psychological issue.

8/S2/F0.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

8/S2/F1.text: Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

8/S2/F2.text: Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

8/S2/F3.text: Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

8/S3/F0.text: Immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide or does provide, and that description can be measured or comprehended.

8/S3/F1.text: Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

8/S3/F2.text: Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

8/S3/F3.text: Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

8/S3/F4.text: The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.

8/S3/F5.text: Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

8/S4/F0.text: Slater and Wilbur's 1997 paper is one of the earliest papers related to virtual reality (VR) immersion and presence, and it is one of the references from which the terms and definitions of immersion and presence were taken.
